Create a finished museum-quality medical educational infographic directly on the image canvas, not a photographed poster, room, desk, screen, or prop mockup. Portrait-oriented composition with one dominant integrated anatomical hero and EIGHT substantial supporting panels. Title: “IRON-DEFICIENCY ANEMIA”; subtitle: “Oxygen delivery under strain”. Sophisticated ivory, deep oxblood, muted teal, and warm copper palette, finely rendered medical illustration, soft volumetric lighting on translucent anatomical structures, precise leader lines, disciplined large readable typography, generous separation between panels, and compact plain-language labels. Dense information with excellent hierarchy, not a sparse school poster. No logos, URLs, bibliography, invented statistics, drug doses, lab thresholds, or universal cure claims.
HERO occupying the central vertical spine: a diverse adult shown as an anatomically plausible translucent upper torso with lungs and heart, and an enlarged continuous blood-vessel cutaway carrying red blood cells toward a stylized tissue destination. Show red biconcave cells with tangible soft membranes and a linked microscopic magnification of hemoglobin/oxygen carriage, schematic rather than invented molecular structure. Label “Hemoglobin carries oxygen” and “Less hemoglobin → reduced oxygen carriage”. Do not imply iron itself is inhaled, that all organs fail, or that oxygen saturation must be low. Place an explicitly labeled schematic arrow connecting iron availability, healthy red-cell production, and oxygen carriage; no unsupported bone-marrow cellular details.
Arrange eight numbered panels in two flanking columns around the integrated hero, with distinct visual mechanisms and concise exact labels:
1. “Inside the blood”: large side-by-side magnified red-cell comparison, typical red cells versus “Often smaller, with paler centers”; clearly mark “Schematic comparison—not a diagnosis”. Use equal field scale, dimensional biconcave shapes and a blood-smear texture inset. Pale centers describe hemoglobin reduction, not empty holes. This is explanatory close-up one.
2. “Where iron is lost”: a two-path diagram with dignified non-graphic heavy-menstrual-bleeding icon and gastrointestinal cutaway inset; labels “Heavy menstrual bleeding”, “GI bleeding”, “Blood loss removes iron”. Small arrow ends at reduced iron stores; avoid a single assumed cause for everyone. Explanatory cutaway two.
3. “Intake and absorption”: food-to-gut schematic with legumes and fortified cereal, an intestinal-wall close-up labeled “Absorption can be impaired”, and two separate contextual labels “Celiac disease” / “Stomach or intestinal surgery”. A thinner intake arrow labeled “Low iron intake can contribute”. Do not imply all anemia is due to diet or draw celiac disease as bleeding. Explanatory close-up three.
4. “Symptoms vary”: three varied adult vignettes with quiet concrete body language and symptom callouts “Fatigue”, “Dizziness”, “Shortness of breath”, “Cold hands and feet”. Clearly display “Mild or moderate cases may have no symptoms”. Avoid representing skin pallor as a universal complexion change.
5. “Tests tell different stories”: an illustrated sample tube and two separate instrument-style result cards, not invented numeric readouts. “CBC: hemoglobin + cell size”; “Ferritin: iron stores”; third short label “Iron studies + history guide evaluation”. A clear comparison bracket states “Iron deficiency can occur WITHOUT anemia”; no red/green self-diagnosis gauge or fixed thresholds. Show a clinician reviewing history rather than a consumer diagnosing from one symptom.
6. “Replace iron—and find the cause”: a clinician-directed branching care diagram with an oral-iron tablet icon labeled “Oral iron is common”, a supervised infusion icon labeled “IV iron in selected cases”, and an upstream cause-search loop labeled “Treat blood loss or absorption problems”. Beneath oral iron write “Upset stomach or constipation can occur”. Under IV path “For poor absorption, intolerance, or severe deficiency”. Use no drug brand, dose, or treatment guarantee. Important smaller callout: “Transfusion: selected severe cases; does not fully correct iron deficiency”.
7. “Support iron intake”: beautifully specific miniature food illustrations—beans with distinct curved seed coats, tofu cubes, a modest lean-meat serving, fortified cereal flakes and dark leafy greens—with a separate sliced-orange illustration. Labels “Iron-rich foods” and “Vitamin C supports absorption”. Footer “Diet supports care; treatment depends on the cause”. No claim that food alone cures established anemia.
8. “Why follow-up matters”: three small distinct contextual drawings—heart silhouette, pregnant adult silhouette, child with caregiver—labeled “Possible heart problems”, “Pregnancy complications”, “Developmental delays in children”. Heading emphasizes “Untreated anemia can have consequences”, not inevitable harm; connect with a thin follow-up arrow to “Clinical evaluation + cause-specific care”.
Overall minimum visible information layers: integrated anatomical hero, red-cell comparison, blood-loss cause/effect branches, intestinal absorption cutaway, diverse symptom context, laboratory distinction, treatment decision diagram, and food-support vignette. At least three explanatory magnified diagrams are prominent, substantive and readable. All arrows and labels must express only the described supported relationships. Keep text short enough to read, rich illustrated surface detail without clutter, and fully fill the designed infographic canvas. Bottom footer in readable type: “General education—not a diagnosis. Discuss symptoms and iron supplements with a clinician.”

claims.claim: Iron deficiency can impair production of healthy red blood cells; low hemoglobin in anemia reduces oxygen carriage from lungs to other organs.
Iron-deficiency anemia can show small red blood cells with pale centers on a blood smear; low mean cellular volume is a common laboratory finding.
Blood loss removes iron; heavy menstrual bleeding and gastrointestinal bleeding are causes requiring evaluation.
Low intake of iron-containing foods can contribute; celiac disease and stomach or intestinal surgery can impair iron absorption.
Mild or moderate iron-deficiency anemia may have no symptoms; more serious disease can cause fatigue, dizziness, pale skin, cold hands and feet, shortness of breath, or chest pain.
Evaluation includes medical and diet history, a complete blood count with hemoglobin and cell size, ferritin, and other iron studies; further testing depends on suspected cause.
Low ferritin indicates reduced iron stores; iron deficiency can occur without anemia, so hemoglobin alone does not establish iron-store status.
Treatment depends on cause and severity; clinician-guided oral iron is common, and intravenous iron may be used for poor absorption, intolerance, severe deficiency, or chronic blood loss.
Oral iron may cause upset stomach or constipation; significant symptoms should be discussed with the treating clinician.
Iron replacement must be paired with finding and treating the underlying cause; transfusion is reserved for selected severe cases and does not completely correct iron deficiency.
Beans, tofu, lean red meat, fortified cereals, and dark leafy greens provide iron; vitamin-C-rich foods such as oranges can support absorption.
Treating blood loss or absorption problems may help prevent iron-deficiency anemia; diet supports iron intake but is not a universal substitute for treatment.
Untreated iron-deficiency anemia may lead to heart problems, pregnancy complications, or developmental delays in children.

claims.claim: The pear-shaped gallbladder lies below the liver in the upper right abdomen and stores bile produced by the liver.
Bile passes through hepatic, cystic and common bile ducts into the duodenum; the pancreas also delivers digestive juices to the duodenum.
Eating signals the gallbladder to release stored bile into the duodenum to mix with food.
Gallstones are hard pebble-like material formed in the gallbladder; cholesterol stones are typically yellow-green and pigment stones are dark and made of bilirubin.

Stones may form when bile has too much cholesterol or bilirubin, insufficient bile salts, or the gallbladder empties incompletely or too infrequently; the reasons for bile changes are not fully understood.
Most gallstones are silent and do not cause symptoms; asymptomatic gallbladder stones usually need no treatment.
A stone obstructing a bile duct can cause bile buildup and biliary colic; attacks often stop when the stone moves and the blockage ends.
Pain can be severe and constant, in the upper right or middle abdomen, last several hours, and accompany nausea or vomiting; attacks often follow heavy meals.
Persistent blockage can lead to gallbladder inflammation, bile-duct infection, or gallstone pancreatitis; these are possible complications, not inevitable outcomes.
Risk is higher with older age, family history, obesity, rapid weight loss, and in women; risk factors do not establish an individual diagnosis.
Evaluation of suspected gallstones can include ultrasound and blood tests; similar symptoms may have other causes requiring clinical assessment.
The main treatment for symptomatic gallstones is gallbladder removal, often laparoscopic; ERCP may clear a stone in the common bile duct. Treatment depends on clinical circumstances.
After gallbladder removal, bile flows from the liver through the ducts directly into the duodenum rather than being stored in a gallbladder.

Healthy eating with fiber, regular physical activity, maintaining a healthy weight and avoiding rapid weight loss can help reduce gallstone risk; they do not guarantee prevention or dissolve existing stones.

Seek urgent medical care for sudden severe abdominal pain, pain lasting several hours, fever or chills, jaundice, or pain spreading to the back with vomiting; dark urine and pale stools may accompany complications.

claims.claim: A cataract is clouding of the natural lens; the normally clear lens bends incoming light to help vision.
The cornea, iris and lens are front-of-eye structures; the pupil is widened by dilation, and the retina and optic nerve are examined at the back of the eye.
The retina is the light-sensitive tissue layer at the back of the eye.
Age-related changes cause lens proteins to break down and clump, creating cloudy areas; most age-related cataracts develop gradually, at variable rates.
Cataracts can affect one or both eyes but do not spread between eyes.

Cloudy or blurry vision, faded or yellowish colors, glare or halos, difficulty seeing at night and ghosted or double images in the affected eye can occur; symptoms can also reflect other eye problems.
Older age, smoking, diabetes, sun exposure, steroid use, family history and previous eye injury are cataract risk factors; these do not establish an individual diagnosis.
Evaluation includes visual acuity or refraction, slit-lamp examination of front-of-eye structures, and a dilated examination to check the eye including retina and optic nerve.
For mild symptoms, updated glasses, brighter reading light and magnification can help function but do not remove the cataract.
Only surgery removes a cataract; the cloudy natural lens is removed and replaced by an artificial intraocular lens (IOL).
Surgery is considered when cataracts interfere with everyday activities; immediate surgery is not always needed, and benefits and risks should be discussed with an ophthalmologist.
UV-protective sunglasses and a brimmed hat, stopping smoking and protective eyewear can help reduce avoidable eye risks; these measures do not guarantee cataract prevention.
Sudden new floaters, flashes, or a curtain or shadow across vision can signal retinal detachment rather than gradual cataract change; seek an eye doctor or emergency room immediately.

claims.claim: Atopic dermatitis is a chronic inflammatory skin disease, often starting in childhood but possible at any age; it is not contagious.
Barrier changes allow moisture to escape and expose the skin immune system to the environment; genes, immune activity and environmental factors contribute, and there is no single known cause.
Skin has a protective outer layer; a schematic intact-versus-disrupted surface comparison illustrates moisture retention versus increased water loss, not a literal hole through the whole skin.
Inflammation can trigger itch; scratching causes further skin damage and inflammation and increases bacterial infection risk.
Symptoms include intense itching, dryness, cracking, scaling and thickened skin; scratches may bleed or weep clear fluid.
Eczema appearance varies with skin tone: it can appear red, purple, grey or lighter or darker than surrounding skin; inflammation may leave color changes.
Common sites include elbow and knee bends and hands; babies often have facial eczema. Distribution varies by age and can occur elsewhere.
Symptoms fluctuate between flares and improvement; itch can disturb sleep.
Family history of eczema, asthma or hay fever is associated with increased likelihood, not proof of one cause.
Soap, detergents, fragrances, rough fabrics, heat and stress may worsen symptoms; triggers vary by person.
Diagnosis involves clinical skin examination and medical, family and trigger history; clinicians may use tests to rule out other causes.
Regular moisturizing, including immediately after bathing, helps retain water and supports the skin barrier; gentle unscented or non-soap cleansing and lukewarm water can help.
Avoid personal irritants, keep cool and keep nails short to reduce scratching damage; do not change diet unless advised by a clinician.

Topical corticosteroids reduce inflammation; other topical treatments, phototherapy or systemic medicines may be considered by clinicians depending on severity, age and response, not as universal treatments.
Treatment can control symptoms but there is currently no cure; seek care for symptoms or treatments that are not helping.

Painful warm swollen skin, pus, sudden worsening or spreading, fever or feeling unwell, and new blisters or leaking/crusting can signal infection or eczema herpeticum and warrant urgent medical advice.
Emollients transferred onto clothing, bedding or dressings can make fabrics catch fire more easily; avoid smoking and naked flames.
